text: JWTs provide the foundation for Row Level Security. Each Supabase product is able to securely decode and verify the validity of a JWT it receives before using Postgres policies and roles to authorize access to the project's data.

The exp field sets a time limit after which the token should not be trusted and is considered expired, even if it is properly signed. The sub field is the unique ID of the user represented by the token.
quote_note: Combines separate exp and sub table entries and rephrases the sub definition.

text: JWTs are strings with the structure header.payload.signature. Each of the three sections is base64url encoded, so a JWT can be transmitted as a single string.
quote_note: Condenses the structure example and its explanation.

text: Supabase Auth continuously issues a new JWT for each user session, for as long as the user remains signed in.
Supabase provides a comprehensive system of managing JWT Signing Keys used to create and verify JSON Web Tokens. Every JWT is signed with a cryptographic key so the token is tamper-resistant.
quote_note: Combines the signing-keys description with the JWT introduction.

text: Postgres Row Level Security (RLS) gives you granular authorization rules that run inside the database.

A table in an exposed schema without RLS is readable and writable by any role with a grant on it. Enable RLS on every table in an exposed schema. On projects that still grant `anon` and `authenticated` by default, revoke those grants. Adding policies doesn't remove them.

section: Understand Row Level Security > What a policy does
text: Think of a policy as adding a WHERE clause to every query. A policy like create policy on todos for select to authenticated using (auth.uid() = user_id) translates to select * from todos where auth.uid() = todos.user_id whenever a user selects from the table.
quote_note: Rephrases the policy example; the SQL in the passage is illustrative, not a direct quotation.

section: Understand Row Level Security > Grants and policies
text: The anon role should keep only what signed-out visitors are meant to read, the authenticated role only the operations your app exposes to signed-in users, and the service_role has full access. service_role bypasses RLS, so keep it server-side.
quote_note: Summarizes the grants table and accompanying service_role guidance.

section: Secure a table with RLS > Call functions with select
text: Wrapping auth functions like (select auth.uid()) causes an initPlan to be run by the Postgres optimizer, which allows it to cache the results per-statement, rather than calling the function once per row.
quote_note: Paraphrases the “Call functions with select” performance guidance.

section: Understand Row Level Security > Grants and policies
text: Adding policies doesn't take those grants back. A table protected only by policies still hands `anon` an insert path if you never revoke the grant.

section: Secure a table with RLS > Run the test suite
text: The procedure for every table in an exposed schema is: set the grants, add the policies, and verify with supabase test db.
quote_note: Summarizes the table-security procedure and test step.

text: Supabase Auth enforces rate limits on endpoints such as sign-up and token refresh to protect projects from abuse; limits are configurable per project.
quote_note: Paraphrase of Supabase Auth rate-limit guidance.

text: A session in Supabase Auth pairs a short-lived access token with a refresh token; when the access token expires, the client uses the refresh token to obtain a new pair.
quote_note: Paraphrase of the session and refresh-token explanation.

text: Signing out can be scoped to the current session, all sessions of the user, or other sessions, and it revokes the affected refresh tokens so they can no longer be used.
quote_note: Summarizes the sign-out scopes and refresh-token revocation behavior.

text: Supabase Auth supports MFA factors such as authenticator-app TOTP and phone codes; a verified second factor is reflected in the session JWT as aal2 assurance.
quote_note: Paraphrases the Overview section; replaces the inaccurate passkeys claim with factors documented by the source.

text: When row security is enabled on a table (with ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY), all normal access to the table for selecting rows or modifying rows must be allowed by a row security policy. If no policy exists for the table, a default-deny policy is used, so that no rows are visible or updatable.
quote_note: Combines and rephrases the RLS-enforcement and default-deny description.

text: The table's owner is typically not subject to row security policies, though a table owner can choose to be subject to row security with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.
quote_note: Paraphrases the table-owner exception and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY behavior.

text: Superusers and roles with the BYPASSRLS attribute always bypass the row security system when accessing a table.
When multiple policies apply to a given query, they are combined using OR for permissive policies, which are the default, or using AND for restrictive policies.
quote_note: Rephrases the OR/AND policy-combination rule.

text: The OR behavior of permissive policies is similar to the rule that a given role has the privileges of all roles that it is a member of.
quote_note: Paraphrases the role-membership analogy.

text: A policy that omits WITH CHECK implicitly provides a WITH CHECK clause identical to its USING clause, so the constraint applies both to rows selected by a command and to rows being inserted or updated.
quote_note: Summarizes the USING/WITH CHECK default behavior.

text: A policy such as CREATE POLICY account_managers ON accounts TO managers USING (manager = current_user) restricts members of the managers role to rows where manager equals the current user.
quote_note: Summarizes the managers policy example.

text: Policies can be specified for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or ALL commands. A policy for ALL applies to every command type.
quote_note: Paraphrases the policy command-scope description.

text: Restrictive policies are combined with AND, so a row must pass every restrictive policy in addition to at least one permissive policy to be visible.
quote_note: Summarizes how restrictive policies combine with permissive policies.

text: When access privileges are granted to a table according to the SQL privilege system but row security is not enabled, all rows within it are equally available for querying or updating.
quote_note: Paraphrases the SQL privilege and no-policy description.

text: Policy expressions run with the privileges of the user issuing the query; security-definer functions can access data unavailable to that user.
quote_note: Paraphrases the privilege context for policy expressions and security-definer functions.

text: RLS expressions normally run before conditions or functions from a user's query; leakproof functions are the exception and may be applied ahead of the row-security check.
quote_note: Paraphrases the planner-order rule and leakproof-function exception.

text: ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY turns the row security policy enforcement off for the table; rows become visible according to ordinary privileges again.
quote_note: Paraphrases the ALTER TABLE reference behavior.

text: CREATE POLICY defines a new row-level security policy for a table. The policy name must be unique per table, and the policy applies to the roles named in its TO clause, or to PUBLIC if no roles are named.
quote_note: Summarizes the CREATE POLICY reference.

text: DROP POLICY removes the specified row-level security policy from a table. Dropping the last policy of a table does not disable row security; the default-deny policy still applies while row security is enabled.
quote_note: Combines the DROP POLICY description and default-deny note.
